script.title: Why Lavoisier sealed burning metal in glass

lines: A French chemist sealed tin inside a glass vessel, then heated it.
Back then, chemists said burning things gave off something called phlogiston.
But when Antoine Lavoisier burned phosphorus, it got heavier.
So in 1774, Lavoisier heated tin and lead in sealed vessels.
He weighed everything inside the glass, so no gas could escape.
The metals still got heavier. They had joined with the air.
That October, Joseph Priestley visited Paris.
Priestley told Lavoisier about an air from heated red mercury powder.
Fire burned in it with extreme vigor.
Lavoisier ran his own tests on it.
You see, it's like a sealed bottle of wine.
The air trapped on top slowly feeds the wine as it uses oxygen.
Lavoisier proved it: burning things combine with part of the air.
In 1778, he named that part oxygen.
And in his sealed glass, the total mass stayed the same.
But Lavoisier also worked for a hated tax company.
Revolutionaries charged him with tax fraud and adding water to tobacco.
In 1794, Lavoisier was guillotined in Paris.
A year and a half later, France cleared him.
His widow got his belongings back, with a note: falsely convicted.
Today, French schools teach his rule: nothing is lost, nothing is created.

claims.claim: When phosphorus burned, it combined with a large quantity of air and the phosphorus increased in weight on burning (late 1772).
Priestley thought phlogiston was given off by burning bodies; he called the new air dephlogisticated air.

In the spring of 1774, Lavoisier carried out experiments on the calcination of tin and lead in sealed vessels, confirming that the increase in weight of metals in combustion was due to combination with air.
He carefully weighed the reactants and products of a chemical reaction in a sealed glass vessel so that no gases could escape; the total mass of matter is the same at the end as at the beginning.

In October Joseph Priestley visited Paris and told Lavoisier of the air he had produced by heating the red calx of mercury, which supported combustion with extreme vigor; Lavoisier carried out his own research on it.
Lavoisier theorized that common air, or one of its components, combines with substances when they are burned, and demonstrated this through experiment.
He named oxygen (1778), recognizing it as an element.
Lavoisier was an administrator of the Ferme generale, a tax farming company that was one of the most hated parts of the Ancien Regime.
He was charged with tax fraud and adding water to tobacco before selling it, and was guillotined on 8 May 1794 in Paris.

A year and a half after his execution, Lavoisier was exonerated by the French government; his belongings were delivered to his widow with a note reading 'To the widow of Lavoisier, who was falsely convicted'.
In France the law of conservation of mass is taught as Lavoisier's Law: 'Nothing is lost, nothing is created, everything is transformed.'
In a sealed wine bottle the headspace functions as an oxygen reserve: as the wine uses oxygen, gas passes from the headspace to the wine.

cast.lavoisier: a 31 year old French chemist, tall and slim, a smooth oval face with a long straight nose and dark arched eyebrows, a white powdered wig tied back with a black silk ribbon, clean shaven, wearing a sky blue silk coat with silver buttons over a white lace jabot, 1770s
cast.priestley: a 41 year old English minister and chemist, short and plump, a round pink face with a double chin and small dark eyes, a short grey curled wig, wearing a plain black wool coat with white clerical neck bands, 1770s
cast.elder: a 60 year old French chemist, thin and stooped, a long wrinkled face with a pointed chin, a tall white powdered wig, wearing a mustard yellow brocade coat with brown cuffs, 1770s
cast.rebel: a 29 year old French revolutionary, lean, a sharp sun-darkened face with a short black beard, a red wool cap with a blue white and red rosette, a striped brown and cream waistcoat over a loose white shirt, 1790s
cast.marie: a 37 year old French woman, slender, a pale oval face with large dark brown eyes, dark brown hair in loose curls under a black lace cap, wearing a black silk mourning gown with a white muslin fichu, 1790s
cast.teacher: a 45 year old French science teacher, a broad friendly face, short curly grey hair, a neat grey beard, round tortoiseshell glasses, wearing a teal knitted cardigan over a white shirt, 2020s
